title: 7 Factors 2 Discernment
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up discernment, the second of the Seven Factors of Awakening, and its Sanskrit name dharmavichaya, "analysis of experience." Nomon links it to mindfulness and to later teachers' translation of the factor as interest, illustrated by James Baraz's story of a college friend who earned top grades by getting curious about why professors loved their subjects. Nomon leads a standing mindful check-in on body, emotion, and thinking, then reads the Buddha's two-arrows and poisoned-arrow passages, where a wounded man refuses a surgeon until he learns the archer's clan and the bowstring's material. Nomon's homework is to notice which of the five hindrances is strongest and meet it with mindfulness.

sentences.text: Good evening.
When I was preparing tonight's talk, it was coming out a little long, so I didn't know if it would fit after service.
That's why no service.
So that's how that went.
Tonight I thought we'd continue our journey through this early Buddhist teaching called the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
Some very clever people have a little sheet from last time, wow.
Seven Factors of Enlightenment, or sometimes called the Seven Factors of Awakening.
I learned it as the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
It's interesting: does a word matter?
It seems like a word matters, enlightenment or awakening.
And I notice my preference is leaning towards awakening between these two.
Coming to see the process of life is pretty much all process.
It might be that life is pretty much all process.
And enlightenment sounds like kind of a state, a state of being.
Before you were not enlightened and then you are enlightened, and there's no backsliding or something.
Like a state change.
Kind of like water.
It's the same person, I suppose, an enlightened person or a not enlightened person, but maybe it's like a state change, the way we think about it.
Water in its liquid form looks really different from water as gas.
It looks different, it feels different from steam.
That's the same thing, right?
It's the same molecule.
It's possible that's the case.
And it seems like we have exemplars in human history and all the cultures of really exceptional people.
So maybe there are enlightened people.
It's possible.

But I think on the whole, whether or not there is such a thing or a state called enlightenment, it's healthier for us, probably, and more skillful to let go of the idea that there could be a state, any state at all.
Or a plane of consciousness or a higher or lower something.
It may be more helpful to think in terms of process, and then awakening is a process.
Awakening is the process of waking up.
There is a change implied.
Being sleepy is different from being wide awake, being really present.
But there's a continuity there, or some gradations perhaps.
Some processes happening in the process of waking up and falling asleep.
And we don't have to feel so bad when we fall asleep again, because we know we'll wake up again.

So as most helpful in this process of awakening, the Buddha suggests that there are seven mental factors that we should focus on, practice with, bring to light, illuminate, give energy and attention to.
We don't need to manufacture them though, because they're all already there to some extent in the human life, in the human heart.
Last week we talked about mindfulness as the first factor.
Tonight we're talking about the second mental factor that furthers this process of awakening.
What's interesting about this factor is it's all about the question of what furthers the process of awakening and what hinders it.
So the second factor is discernment, discerning.
Which actions of body, speech and mind, which tendencies, which leanings, which habits support awakening, and which diminish awakening and put us back to sleep, back into suffering.
Discernment is the most common translation of this term.
The Sanskrit is dharmavichaya, dharmavichaya.
And like everything in this teaching, it's about actually paying a lot more attention to our inner experience on a moment by moment, immediate basis.
Not some idea of how we're doing or some sense of how we're doing, but what's happening now, what's happening now.
The Sanskrit term dharmavichaya is a compound word.
The first part is dharma, and this is the little d-dharma that stands for experience, atoms of experience or moments, units of experience.
The second half, vichaya, means analysis.
So analysis of experience is what the word means, really literally.
But if we were to say analysis of experience, it sounds very heady.
Like I'm going to figure out my experience.
And it seems like the harder we try to figure out the experience, the more screwed up we get.
So probably that very idea of discernment as figuring out something might be a little bit self-defeating.
In the early texts of Buddhism, the way this dharmavichaya, this discernment, is described is a kind of analysis, though.
It's really paying attention to cause and effect as an analytical tool.
I think when we think analysis, we think of things in fixed categories: we're going to figure out which category this unknown thing belongs in, this category or that category.
It has this element.

But the way they understood analysis in early Buddhism was that nothing really fits in any category, but some things lead to other things, or some things are associated with or support other things happening.
This arises with that, and this doesn't arise with that.
So things come together in constellations of causes and conditions.
They're really interested in what leads to what.
We seem to be interested in some rigid, fixed categorization, and they were interested in how you describe the flow and understand the flow.
Sometimes maybe we should think of our life as a river.
Why do we throw that enormous hunk of concrete in the middle of our river?
We're in the river really flowing smoothly, and we're the back eddies and so on.

So anyway, what they wanted to analyze when they were looking at this dharmavichaya was: what are the things that happen in the body, in the mind, when we speak, that lead to release from suffering, that lead to more joy, that lead to more kindness, that lead to awakening?
And what are the things that lead to the opposite?
What leads to more suffering or less suffering?
Or sometimes we say, what's wholesome and what's unwholesome?
And the idea is that we can't tell intrinsically by looking at the qualities or the colors or the shapes or the names for things.
We can only tell by looking at the results.
So that's a little different frame than that.
This is really good to think about, looking at the results.
Oh, that led to more suffering, or that led to less suffering.
And remember that the first factor of awakening was mindfulness.
So these two are going to work together.
There's a sense of a progression here, one thing supporting the next.
And so let's just remember for a second what mindfulness is.
It's a word much in the air.
Mindfulness is paying more attention to the particularities of present moment experience.
The Buddha described mindfulness practice as having four areas of focus.
So it's good to keep these four areas in mind and check ourselves out.
Are we paying attention to all these areas?
Are we stuck in one all the time?
Or none?
The first area of focus is the body.
The first foundation of mindfulness is the body.
So we ask: how does the body really feel?
Where is the body?
What is our attitude about the body?
What is the experience of being in a body?
In that category they include breath awareness.
It's an incredibly helpful tool.
It shows up in all practices, I think, to some extent.
And then the second area of mindfulness is to look at what comes in through the senses beyond the body.
What's coming in through the senses, and how are we reacting and responding in a low-level, before-thought kind of way?
I like that.
Pleasant and unpleasant, positive and negative.
We're attracted to what we're held by.
We notice that moment by moment from the senses.
The eyes take in some information.
The ears hear something.
You smell something.
There's some experience.
And that includes actually noticing a thought arising, but that's a more complicated story.
Let's just think about the senses, and actually notice what we are sensing.
What are we sensing?
So quickly the mind generalizes and flattens things out, right?
A later philosophy of Buddhism, the Yogacara philosophy, said that there are three problems with thinking.
I was just thinking of one of them.
One of the three problems with thinking is flattening.
They call it flattening.
It's this incredibly useful tool we have of taking a word or a concept to represent a vast range of experience.
But the result of that useful, handy tool of using concepts to flatten out experiences is that we miss most of experience.
An example might be a tree.
I mean not a tree, but the word tree, the concept tree.

If you look around in your experience and you look at trees (I brought this up at Sandwich, where there are lots of trees, last weekend, but we can look at this), this thing we call a tree has a million different expressions, right?
One looks this way, one looks that way, one has this kind of leaves, that kind of shape, one is evergreen.
Trees are incredibly diverse, but we just use this one word, tree, to stand for this incredible diversity of experience.
We do that with everything else too.
We flatten things out with our concepts.
In a way that's useful and important.
If you're asking somebody to go wait under the tree, it's good if we all agree that's a tree.
But to actually look at a tree, and actually look at our experience: you can think of the different ways that you do this flattening.
That's why it's helpful to reinvigorate our attention to what's actually coming in through the senses, and how this mind-body organism responds just instantly.
We probably do that with trees too, for I like some trees more than other trees.
The third area of mindfulness is to pay attention to the thinking and emotions that get elaborated out of that process.
I like this kind of tree, it's a great tree.
I know all about it, it's deciduous, something like this.
And how do we do that with everything else, including other people?
I know exactly what she's like.
So that's a thought.
Some sensation happened.
I looked and I saw some shape of colors and forms that I identified as Elizabeth.
And then thoughts arise, right?
Thoughts arise, and I notice that process.
Of course it's very pleasant to look at Elizabeth in this moment.
These things change.
Another time they won't be so pleasant, who knows.
It depends on what's going on with me and with Elizabeth and with the rest of the world.
So we notice the thinking that arises and the feelings, the emotions that arise.
And then the fourth is: how does all of this, so you see us getting more and more elaborate, right?
We're such elaborate beings.
How does this elaboration lead to even bigger patterns, habits?
I mean, how do we get into this mess, right?
We have habits and patterns instead of being mindful of those.
In the Buddhist description of this fourth foundation of mindfulness, he didn't really talk about psychological habits or personality.
I don't know if they had that concept exactly in his time.
But he brought up some of the lists that he has used to describe patterns and habits, like the Four Noble Truths.
He brings that up: look at your life reflected by the Four Noble Truths.
What is suffering, the actual experience of suffering, and so on.
And then, as I mentioned last week, a couple of the other habits he mentioned, or patterns of existence, I guess it may be better, we're not habits.
Patterns of existence are the five hindrances and the seven factors of awakening.
So there the first one includes all of them.
Kind of weird.
All of this is, in a way, an antidote to our incredibly compelling me-ness, right?
What if we drop the idea that the organizing principle is me and look instead at experience with different points of view and frames?
When we do that, what we get is a lot more information.

What we get is a lot more information about what's happening, beyond our opinion of what's happening or what we think is happening through our flattening process: what a terrible day, what a great day, whatever.
That's a flattened day, right?
Say, oh, I had a great day.
That was a day that's been flattened.
Or the same with a terrible day, right?
Of course it wasn't just a great day.
It was a rich day, with how many millions of moments happening.

But anyway, as we're becoming more aware of what's happening, and returning to this moment, what's happening, what's happening, then it gives us more information and we can practice the second factor.
They help each other.
Discernment.
Like, now that I notice, now that I cognize Elizabeth and have some feeling for Elizabeth, where do I go from there?
What's wholesome here?
What's helpful, to smile?
Yeah, what's wholesome here?
Or to just be like, I've got stuff to do, I'm going to ignore Elizabeth?
Which is what I usually do.
Sorry.
But it's a habit, right?
So there's mindfulness and there's discernment: what leads to what?
This requires some reflection too, like, huh.
After I left the room, how do I feel now?
Ah.
I just blew right past Elizabeth when I was saying hello.
Ah.
Doesn't feel too good.
So mindfulness provides the material for the second factor of discernment.
And the operative idea is, where should we put our energies?

One of the ways they describe this process of discernment, and they also talk about this in working with the five hindrances, is that we have some choices around what we give energy to and what we don't give energy to.
They talk about it in terms of starving and feeding.
They use that metaphor in the early Buddhist teachings.
I was going to bring an excerpt for that, but I forgot.
Next time.
We have a little bit the frame of controlling, right?
It might be that these things can't be controlled in that way, but maybe we can have some influence over what we feed and what we starve.
So now let's just remember what the five hindrances are.
I'm so happy I've found a way to remember these.
So hopefully this will help you.
You've got a mnemonic going, that's cool.
I've been thinking about them lately in terms of two pairs and doubt.
Like, doubt is [unclear: "social for everything"].
So the two pairs, the first pair, and I changed the wording a little bit so that they would be easier to remember, but it's the same ideas.
These are pretty close to the original.
The first pair is desire and aversion: we're grabbing onto things and pushing things away.
The second pair is dullness or sleepiness and restlessness.
So the first two are this powerful habit of what we want and what we don't want, and the second two are about energy.
Are we too dull, too sleepy, not putting up energy in our life, or are we too like, ah, ah, ah, too restless, too jaggy?
And then doubt: doubting ourself, doubting the practice, doubting our choices.
So we're doing this discernment and we're trying to make choices.
This is actually about making choices.
Subtle choices, moment to moment, we're doing this discernment.
I'm going to put more energy into friendliness, less energy into getting shit done.
It might be something that I practice with my discernment.
But then doubt arises, like, oh, I'm tired.
Am I getting enough done?
Maybe Elizabeth doesn't like me anyway.
Right, doubt arises.
Very generous of you.
Let me use you as an example tonight.
I think I am.
Yeah, I know you can.
So doubt is there.
This discernment and the mindfulness happen in the shadow of the five hindrances, right?
Or you could say they illuminate the five hindrances so that the shadows get wiped out and the five hindrances lose their power.
In all of early Buddhism, he talks a lot about the incredible power of just recognizing things, incredible power of just recognizing things.
We don't necessarily need to fix or improve, but just to recognize something.
All the time the five hindrances are personified in this character who shows up named Mara.
I'll try to remember to bring a Mara passage next week too.
Usually what happens is Mara is whispering sweet nothings in the Buddha's ear about how messed up, negative stuff.
And the Buddha's power is that you can turn towards Mara and say, oh, I see you.
And then Mara goes drat, and stomps out, because Mara has been seen.
So these hindrances and these doubts operate partly because we're not really so aware of them, right?
We're hearing this voice in our head: I'm not a good person, I don't have energy, I'm never going to figure this out.
My economic problems, my personal problems, my relationship problems, oh yeah.
And so the Buddha is saying, with these factors of awakening, the first two things are to notice what's happening and discern, and to recognize, to see, oh, that's doubt.
Now what do I do?
Maybe nothing.
I don't need to do anything but see that.
So the early commentators, looking at this factor of discernment, talked a lot about being more aware of what's happening and then discerning.
Should I do this, should I do that?
What leads to more joy, what leads to more suffering?
But it sounds a little mechanical to us.

What's interesting is that the later, modern commentators that I've read or downloaded, listened to, zapped into my brain through the internet, are mostly translating the second factor as interest, which is interesting, literally.
Yeah, instead of discernment, interest, and interest in terms of getting more interested, being more interested, bringing up interestedness, or maybe you could say curiosity about experience.
What's really happening here?

So it's sort of like supporting, like they're saying, really we need to support mindfulness more with interest and with curiosity, and worry a little bit less about whether you can figure something out or make all these minute choices that early Buddhism seems to be calling for.
So that's interesting.
And it can be sort of mundane, worldly, big-picture things.
It could be moment-by-moment things.
I was listening to this talk by James Baraz, who's a Vipassana teacher.
He visited here one time, actually.
Really nice guy.
He sang songs to us to become, yeah, anyway.
And in this talk by James Baraz, he was telling a story about when he was in college with a friend of his.
He said he and his friend, a friend from high school, had been completely on the same track through high school.
They'd gotten the same grades, taken the same classes, just been buddies.
But when they got to college, his friend just took off.
He took all the advanced honors classes and got incredible grades and graduated summa cum laude, or however you pronounce that, and went on to be a well-regarded professor.
He said, he asked us, he talked to me, like he realized this about their senior year, that something had changed.
And he was still kind of a B-plus student, hanging around.
And he asked his friend, "Well, how come you're doing so much better than me, do you think?
Are you actually smarter than me?"
We didn't realize it at first.

And his friend said, "Well, you know what I thought of as soon as we started college was how interesting it is that these professors would choose to devote their life to this subject, even if at first it might seem to me like a really boring, dry, uninteresting thing.
And so throughout college, I've been more and more interested in that question: why would somebody love statistics or economics so much?
And so my whole college career I've been just trying to figure that out, trying to sort of get in the head space of the professors.
And as a result, I naturally got interested in the material and did all the reading and got good grades."
So that was an interesting example: just getting interested, just getting interested.
And that's kind of an external thing, getting interested in academic studies or something like that, but it also means getting interested in our life.
What's really happening in our life, and how interesting that is.
And so meditation supports this.
If we bring up this quality of curiosity and interest in meditation, that supports this also.
So that's why I said those words during Zazen.
This is, in a way, an investigation, or a questioning: oh, what is it?
What is it to be really present?
What is it to feel the breath and feel the body and to notice thoughts coming and going?
How interesting.
Although, on the same token, I remember at one point Norman used to say, yeah, it's great to get more interested in the mind, but not too interested.
So we don't want to get too ingrown, obsessed, like, "Oh, wow, I want better, more thoughts, cool thoughts."
It's still just thoughts.
It's just experience.
It's just a body.
It's not that interesting.
But it is interesting, so it's interesting to walk these lines.
But it's an embodied practice, so not just a way of thinking or a philosophy.
And so this term, I find thinking about interest as a nice bridge, if we can think about interest as in between one and two, like a bridge, bridging mindfulness and discernment.
Sort of being interested: what's the information from mindfulness?
And how can I discern these tendencies, these leanings, these choices that are happening all the time?
Can I work with them a little more skillfully?
And then it goes on just immediately to the next one, which is diligence.
And onto the next one after that, which is joy.
As we get interested and are able to discern a little more, if it all is working well, the way the Buddha recommended, we get some positive feedback.
The loop's going right.
We feel a little better.
We have a little more energy.
So naturally we're a little more diligent.
We wake up in the morning, and we're like, "Oh, I don't totally feel like sitting, but it's so interesting to go sit."
I'm like, "Oh, I'm going to go sit.
It feels good."
And then joy emerges, and then the rest of the factors spool out from there.
So I thought I might share with you a practice that I invented for the mindfulness classes called the mindful check-in.
So we have to step out for a moment from our formal dharma talk mode and stand up.
And just feel free to stretch a little bit.
So we're touching into the body here, from the bodied life.
Kind of surreal, how that world peace might be attained if every workplace had a 20-minute stretch break every 20 minutes.
Stretch break.
The body, not the body.
It's still this long, isn't it?
So anyway, if you're a little bit, I don't feel a big, good routine, but just kind of give yourself back to yourself.
And then really stand to feel the weight of the feet on the floor.
Feel the presence of the body.
You have the hands dangling or in shashu, either way.
And so the mindful check-in is a deliberate application of these different frames of mindfulness.
You could do it in any posture, but I think standing is good, because we're not used to standing.
Either we're sitting, working away, collapsed, lying down, or walking someone to get something open.
So standing is something we don't associate with all these activities.
So it's sort of a freed-up posture.
So to really stop and stand.
And then to make an inquiry in three areas.
The first is: what are the sensations in the body right now?
What do you notice if you just touch into the feeling in the body?
Might be particular sensations.
You can just notice the mass of sensations, the feeling tone of the body, just of the body.
And you actually feel like you're breathing.
You'll notice when the mind wanders away, and bring it back.
What are the sensations in the body right now?
That's the first thing.
And then move the focus to emotion.
Now this is easy, although I'm not talking to you, but just learning the form and practices during the day.
But just to be curious: what are the emotions, or the emotion?
Are there nameable emotion states happening?
Is there a non-verbal feeling for what the emotion is right now?
We don't always notice emotion because it really [unclear: "clears up"].
What's happening with emotion?
A little bit.
What's happening with emotion?
And then the third and the last one, probably the most of those I'm talking to you, let's see what you can do, is thinking itself.
What you can notice about thinking.
Particular dominant thoughts.
Patterns of thinking.
Thinking dull and sticky or jagged.
Very rapid and elaborated.
So check in softer in the day.
Check in.
What's the thinking?
That's the third question.
Do this in a minute or two.
Nobody even has to know that you're doing a mindful check-in.
Do something like that at home.
Walking around the city, waiting for a stop sign.
It's a stopping and checking in, but then it helps you bring up some questions like that.
How am I doing?
I have so many individual answers to that.
This is investigating experience with these different dimensions from the foundations of mindfulness.
So thank you for trying that.
And then we have information for our discernment.
One of the major things that the Buddha talked a lot about is: what are we adding?
What are we adding to experience?
There's experience, and then the mind has an incredible ability to add all kinds of stuff, right?
Judgment, elaboration, fear.
And one of the ways the Buddha taught, the Buddha had two connected stories about what we add to experience, or how we process experience, how we discern our relations to experience.
He had two related stories that both use arrows as metaphors.
Many of us probably have heard before these very popular Buddhist stories.
It was mixed together in the popular press.
So we were worried about gun violence.
They must have been worried about arrow violence in that day.
The first story about the arrows is the story of the second arrow, or the second dart, sometimes as translated.
And the idea of this one, and this is a discernment-to-mindfulness thing, is that we can become more aware of how we do this and not do it as much.
So the idea is that something difficult is going to happen, right?
That's baked into experience.
There's pain and difficulty as part of experience.
And that's the first arrow.
An arrow hits us.
Pain in the knee, a painful memory, somebody looks at us like anything, something painful.
And we now know from the super geniuses doing all the neuroscience work that internally there's very little difference between physical and emotional pain.
It activates the same regions of the brain.
So something happens to us.
And then somehow the minute we experience something painful, says the Buddha, we can incredibly quickly grab our own bow and arrows, turn it around and shoot ourselves with a second arrow.
Here's how the Buddha described it.
*The Blessed One said, "When touched with a feeling of pain, the uninstructed, run-of-the-mill person sorrows, grieves and laments, beats her breast, becomes distraught.
And so she feels two pains, physical and mental, just as if they were to shoot a man with an arrow, and right afterwards were to shoot him with another one, so he would feel the pain of two arrows.
In the same way, when touched with a feeling of pain, the uninstructed, run-of-the-mill person"*
So somebody who doesn't practice this stuff,
*sorrows, grieves and laments, beats his breast, becomes distraught.
And so he feels two pains, physical and mental.*
Or we could also say mental and mental.
So judgment, self-doubt, there's a menu, right?
You know what these are.
One of the discernment practices is to notice that happening.

Because we're a little more dropped into our present moment experience through our mindfulness practice, and we're interested in how we're responding to things and what leads to what, when something happens we can a little more often discern: oh, that was really painful, I really feel such and such a feeling.
And I notice this desire to add additional weight and theme and judgment and all the stuff on top of it, right?
And maybe, with discernment, I can instead notice the body.
Instead I could breathe.
Instead I could do something with attention so that I don't do that, or don't do it as much.
So that's the story of the two arrows.
The second story is the story of the poisoned arrow.
This is another way of describing our unskillful responses to difficulty.
In the second story, the metaphor is that a really nasty thing happened to you.
You got shot by a poisoned arrow.
This is maybe a little worse than the first arrow of the two.
This is a really bad arrow.
A big poisoned arrow.
It really hurts, something that you really don't like happens.
And in the metaphor, your friends notice you've been shot by a poisoned arrow, and they want to pull the arrow out.
They want to help you.
Or you could say you want to help yourself.
There's a desire on the one hand to get this arrow out.
To process this wound.
To heal.
To move on.
To say ouch and just move on.
What the story points out is we don't always do that.
We get a little bit obsessed with the arrow.
Why did this happen to me?
What kind of arrow is that anyway?
Hey, Did you shoot that arrow, or did you shoot that arrow?
Meanwhile our friends are saying, "It's poison, get it out!"
Here's how the Buddha puts it.
This one's really cute.
The Buddha goes into a lot of detail to make his point.
*It's just as if a man was wounded by an arrow that was thickly smeared with poison.
His friends and companions, kinsmen and relatives, want to provide him with a surgeon.
But the man would say, I won't have this arrow removed until I know whether the man who wounded me was a noble warrior, a Brahmin, a merchant or a worker.
And he would say, I will not have this arrow removed until I know the given name and clan name of the man who wounded me.
Until I know whether he was tall, medium or short.
Until I know whether he was dark, ruddy brown, golden colored.
Until I know his hometown, village or city.
Until I know whether the bow with which I was wounded was a long bow or a crossbow.
Until I know whether the bow string with which I was wounded was fiber, bamboo threads, sinew, hemp or bark.*
This is like a 2000-year-old joke.
*Until I know whether the shaft with which I was wounded was wild or cultivated.
Until I know whether the feathers of the shaft with which I was wounded were made from a vulture, made from a stork, made from a hawk, made from a peacock or some other bird.
Until I know whether the shaft with which I was wounded was bound with the sinew of an ox, a water buffalo, a langur or a monkey.
He would say, I will not have this arrow removed until I know whether the shaft with which I was wounded was that of a common arrow, a curved arrow, a barbed or a calf tooth, or an oleander arrow.
This man would die.*
And then he concludes: this man would die.
So this is a process of mindfulness and discernment.
Something happens to us.
Are we willing to move on?
Are we willing to say "ouch," respond in some way that seems skillful, and move on?
Or are we obsessed with our wound, obsessed with the arrow?
Are we working in the realms of blame and judgment and so on and so forth?
Isn't that funny?
So the last thing I want to say about discernment, and then we'll close, is that all of this work involves quite a bit of imagination.

When I think of these things as somewhat dry processes of personality or spiritual growth, whatever you think that means, I was thinking about this, and I think it actually is quite an imaginative act to think that we could have a different mind.
We're quite habituated to our mind the way it is.
So it's an act of imagination to think, wow, there could be less suffering.
There could be more joy.
There could be the possibility of being hit by an arrow and just pulling it out.
"Ouch, okay.
That was an arrow."
So this requires some imagination.
It's a kind of deep reframing of experience itself.
Not only do we think we know who we are, we think we know what reality is.
It's sort of an imaginary act to wonder: is reality really the way I think it is?
Might it be some other way that doesn't lead to so much suffering?
And so there's two levels of work here with our habitual view.
